children.translated_text: May <s>Sarasvatī</s>, all white, long delight in my mind, she who is the female swan in the grove of the lotus-mouths of the four-faced god.
May <s>Sarasvatī</s>, all white, long delight in my mind.
Having gathered together earlier treatises and observed actual usages,
we compose, according to our ability, an account of the characteristics of <s>kāvya</s> (poetry).
Here, for the instructed and for those instructed by the learned, and indeed for learned people in every way,
the conduct of worldly life proceeds only through the clarity of words.

children.text: idam andhaṃ tamaḥ kṛtsnaṃ jāyeta bhuvanatrayam
children.translated_text: This whole threefold world would become blind darkness

children.text: yadi śabdāhvayaṃ jyotir āsaṃsāraṃ na dīpyate ||
children.translated_text: if the light called speech did not shine as long as the world endures.
Having reached literature, the mirror that reflects the fame of ancient kings,

children.text: teṣām asaṃnidhāne 'pi na svayaṃ paśya naśyati ||
children.translated_text: even in their absence, see: it does not perish by itself.

children.text: gaur gauḥ kāmadughā samyak prayuktā smaryate budhaiḥ
children.translated_text: The cow, the cow, when properly employed, is remembered by the wise as wish-fulfilling;

children.text: duṣprayuktā punar gotvaṃ prayoktuḥ saiva śaṃsati ||
children.translated_text: but when wrongly employed, that very cow proclaims only the cowhood of the speaker.

children.text: tad alpam api nopekṣyaṃ kāvye duṣṭaṃ kathaṃcana
children.translated_text: Therefore even a small fault in poetry is never to be disregarded in any way;

children.text: syād vapuḥ sundaram api śvitreṇaikena durbhagam ||
children.translated_text: even a beautiful body becomes unfortunate through a single white leprous spot.
How can a man who does not know the science distinguish merits and faults?
Does a blind man have authority in perceiving differences of form?
Therefore, with the cultivation of people in view, the wise
composed the rules of practice for the varied paths of speech.

children.text: taiḥ śarīraṃ ca kāvyānām alaṃkārāś ca darśitāḥ
children.translated_text: By them both the body of poems and their ornaments have been shown.
First, the body is a sequence of words delimited by the intended meaning.

children.text: padyaṃ gadyaṃ ca miśraṃ ca tat tridhaiva vyavasthitam
children.translated_text: It is arranged in just three forms: verse, prose, and mixed composition.

children.text: padyaṃ catuṣpadī tac ca vṛttaṃ jātir iti dvidhā ||
children.translated_text: Verse is four-footed, and that is of two kinds, <s>vṛtta</s> and <s>jāti</s>.
All its arrangement has been set out in the <s>Chandoviciti</s>.

children.text: sā vidyā naur vivikṣūṇāṃ gambhīraṃ kāvyasāgaram ||
children.translated_text: That science is a boat for those wishing to cross the deep ocean of poetry.

children.text: muktakaṃ kulakaṃ kośaḥ saṃghāta iti tādṛśaḥ
children.translated_text: <s>Muktaka</s>, <s>kulaka</s>, <s>kośa</s>, and <s>saṃghāta</s> are of that sort;
because they are forms that are parts of a canto-composition, the expansion of verse has not been separately stated.
A canto-composition is called a <s>mahākāvya</s> (great poem); its defining marks are these.
Its opening may be a blessing, an act of homage, or a statement of the subject.
It arises from a historical tale or otherwise has a noble basis;
it depends on the fruits of the four human aims and has a clever and exalted hero.
It is adorned with descriptions of cities, oceans, mountains, seasons, and the rising of moon and sun,
with garden scenes, water sports, drinking of wine, and festivals of love,
with separations in love, weddings, and descriptions of the birth of princes,
and also with counsel, messengers, expeditions, battles, and the hero's rise to prosperity.
It is ornamented, not too brief, and continuously filled with rasa and emotion,
with cantos not excessively long, in meters pleasing to hear, and with good transitions.
Everywhere furnished with varied episodes and pleasing to the world,
poetry, richly ornamented, comes into being and endures beyond an age.

children.text: nyūnam apy atra yaiḥ kaiścid aṅgaiḥ kāvyaṃ na duṣyati
children.translated_text: Even if some of these elements are lacking, a poem is not thereby spoiled,
provided that excellence in the elements that have been adopted satisfies those who know the art.

children.text: guṇataḥ prāg upanyasya nāyakaṃ tena vidviṣām
children.translated_text: First presenting the hero by his merits, and then, through him,
the overthrow of his enemies: this path is naturally beautiful.
After describing even the enemy's lineage, valor, learning, and the like,
the description of the hero's superiority through victory over him delights us.
A continuous run of words without metrical feet is prose: <s>ākhyāyikā</s> and <s>kathā</s>

children.text: iti tasya prabhedau dvau tayor ākhyāyikā kila ||
children.translated_text: are said to be its two divisions; of these, the <s>ākhyāyikā</s>, so they say,
is to be narrated by the hero himself, while the other may be narrated by the hero or by someone else.
Revealing one's own virtues is no fault here, since the narrator reports what actually happened.

children.text: api tv aniyamo dṛṣṭas tatrāpy anyair udīraṇāt
children.translated_text: But no fixed rule is observed, because even there narration by others is found.

children.text: anyo vaktā svayaṃ veti kīdṛg vā bhedalakṣaṇam ||
children.translated_text: Another may be the speaker, or oneself; what sort of defining difference is that?

children.text: vaktraṃ cāparavaktraṃ ca socchvāsatvaṃ ca bhedakam
children.translated_text: If <s>vaktra</s>, <s>aparavaktra</s>, and division into <s>ucchvāsa</s> sections

children.text: cihnam ākhyāyikāyāś cet prasaṅgena kathāsv api ||
children.translated_text: are the distinguishing marks of an <s>ākhyāyikā</s>, then by context they occur in stories too.
Why should there not be an entrance of <s>vaktra</s> and <s>aparavaktra</s>, as with <s>āryā</s> and the rest?

children.text: bhedaś ca dṛṣṭo lambhādir ucchvāso vāstu kiṃ tataḥ ||
children.translated_text: And a division such as <s>lambha</s> is seen; or let there be <s>ucchvāsa</s>: what follows from that?
Therefore <s>kathā</s> and <s>ākhyāyikā</s> are one class marked by two names.
The remaining kinds of narratives will be included within this very class.
Abductions of maidens, battles, separations in love, rises to fortune, and the like
are the same as in a canto-composition; these are not distinctive qualities.
A mark created by a poet's imagination is not faulty elsewhere either.

children.text: mukham iṣṭārthasaṃsiddhyai kiṃ hi na syāt kṛtātmanām ||
children.translated_text: For the successful attainment of the desired meaning, what could not serve as an opening for disciplined poets?
Mixed works, such as dramas and the like, are treated at length elsewhere.
A certain composition made of prose and verse is called <s>campū</s>.

children.text: tad etad vāṅmayaṃ bhūyaḥ saṃskṛtaṃ prākṛtaṃ tathā
children.translated_text: This literature, moreover, is said by noble authorities to be fourfold:

children.text: apabhraṃśaś ca miśraṃ cety āhur āryāś caturvidham ||
children.translated_text: Sanskrit, Prākrit, Apabhraṃśa, and mixed.

children.text: saṃskṛtaṃ nāma daivī vāg anvākhyātā maharṣibhiḥ
children.translated_text: Sanskrit is the divine speech explained by the great seers.
The course of Prākrit is manifold, consisting of derivative, identical, and regional forms.
They regard the language based in <s>Mahārāṣṭra</s> as the excellent Prākrit,
a sea of jewels of good sayings, of which works such as the <s>Setubandha</s> are composed.

children.text: śaurasenī ca gauḍī ca lāṭī cānyā ca tādṛśī
children.translated_text: <s>Śaurasenī</s>, <s>Gauḍī</s>, <s>Lāṭī</s>, and other such languages

children.text: yāti prākṛtam ity evaṃ vyavahāreṣu saṃnidhim ||
children.translated_text: also come into common usage under the name Prākrit.
The speech of the <s>Ābhīras</s> and others is remembered in poems as Apabhraṃśa;
in the treatises, anything other than Sanskrit is described as Apabhraṃśa.
Sanskrit includes canto-compositions and the like; Prākrit includes <s>skandhaka</s> and similar forms;
Apabhraṃśa includes <s>osara</s> and the like, while drama and similar works are mixed.
A story too may be composed in all languages and also in Sanskrit;
they call the <s>Bṛhatkathā</s>, made in the <s>Bhūtabhāṣā</s>, a tale of marvelous meaning.
The other kind, such as dance, dramatic gesture, and flashing lightning-like display, is for viewing;

children.text: śravyam eveti saiṣāpi dvayī gatir udāhṛtā ||
children.translated_text: but it is only to be heard. Thus this twofold course too has been stated.

children.text: asty aneko girāṃ mārgaḥ sūkṣmabhedaḥ parasparam
children.translated_text: There are many paths of speech, mutually divided by subtle differences.
Among them the Vaidarbha and Gauḍīya styles are described, since their distinction is clear.
Compactness, lucidity, evenness, sweetness, delicacy,
clarity of meaning, elevation, vigor, charm, and concentration:

children.text: iti vaidarbhamārgasya prāṇā daśa guṇāḥ smṛtāḥ
children.translated_text: these ten qualities are remembered as the life-breaths of the Vaidarbha style.
Their opposites are generally observed on the Gauḍa path.
What is compact has no touch of looseness and is mostly made of consonants of slight breath;
what is loose is, for example, 'a garland of jasmine crowded with restless bees.'
Because of their concern for alliteration, the Gauḍas approve that, on account of the heaviness of the composition;
the Vaidarbhas would pass over it as 'a jasmine wreath crossed by bees.'
Speech is lucid when its meaning is well known and when it wins recognition, as in:
'The dark mark of the moon spreads the beauty of the blue lotus.'
Even what is not very established is approved by the Gauḍīyas as learned usage,
as in, 'the white-rayed one whose mark resembles the lotus-born who was not Arjuna.'
Evenness in compositions is the absence of unevenness. Those compositions are soft, clear, and intermediate,
being produced by arrangements of letters that are soft, clear, or mixed.
'The Malaya breeze comes to me, talkative with the calls of cuckoos,
sprinkled by drops of water from waterfalls clear with leaping spray.'
'The gentle Malaya wind, fragrant from intimacy with sandalwood,
contends with the breaths from fair women's mouths, whose ardent courage is checked.'
Without considering this unevenness, but looking to the pomp of meaning and ornament,
the eastern poetic manner grew.

children.text: madhuraṃ rasavad vāci vastuny api rasasthitiḥ
children.translated_text: Sweetness is that by which intelligent people are intoxicated by speech rich in rasa,
and also by the presence of rasa in the subject, like bees by honey.
Whatever is experienced as similar by whatever kind of sound,
a closeness of words of that form, accompanied by alliteration, is productive of rasa.

children.text: eṣa rājā yadā lakṣmīṃ prāptavān brāhmaṇapriyaḥ
children.translated_text: 'When this king, dear to brahmins, obtained royal fortune,
from then onward there was a festival of <s>dharma</s> in this world.'

children.text: itīdaṃ nādṛtaṃ gauḍair anuprāsas tu tatpriyaḥ
children.translated_text: This is not valued by the Gauḍas; alliteration, however, is dear to them.

children.text: anuprāsād api prāyo vaidarbhair idam iṣyate ||
children.translated_text: The Vaidarbhas generally prefer this even to alliteration.

children.text: varṇāvṛttir anuprāsaḥ pādeṣu ca padeṣu ca
children.translated_text: Alliteration is the recurrence of sounds in pādas and in words,
if the nearness awakens impressions from a previous perception.
'In the moon, the ornament of an autumn night, appearing like a cluster of jasmine,
the dark mark, like a sapphire, establishes beauty.'

children.text: cāru candramasaṃ bhīru bimbaṃ paśyaitad ambare
children.translated_text: 'Timid one, look at this lovely disk of the moon in the sky,
ready pitilessly to kill my mind, overrun by Love.'
They desire alliteration whose sound is not too far separated,
but not such as, 'the moon is like the lotus of a woman's face.'

children.text: smaraḥ kharaḥ khalaḥ kāntaḥ kāyaḥ kopaś ca naḥ kṛśaḥ
children.translated_text: 'Love is harsh, wicked, beloved; our body and anger are thin;

children.text: cyuto māno 'dhiko rāgo moho jāto 'savo gatāḥ ||
children.translated_text: pride has fallen, passion has increased, delusion has arisen, and our lives are gone.'
Such harshness of composition falls into slackness as well;
therefore the southerners do not employ alliteration in this way.
They know yamaka to be repetition whose range is a cluster of sounds.

children.text: tat tu naikāntamadhuram ataḥ paścād vidhāsyate ||
children.translated_text: But that is not absolutely sweet; therefore it will be treated later.

children.text: kāmaṃ sarvo 'py alaṃkāro rasam arthe niṣiñcati
children.translated_text: Granted, every ornament infuses rasa into the meaning;
nevertheless freedom from vulgarity bears this burden most of all.

children.text: kanye kāmayamānaṃ māṃ na tvaṃ kāmayase katham
children.translated_text: 'Girl, why do you not desire me, who desire you?'
This vulgar essence of meaning is arranged so as to cause distaste.
'Granted, the outcaste <s>Kandarpa</s> is pitiless toward me, lotus-eyed one;
by good fortune he is not envious toward you.' This non-vulgar meaning brings rasa.
Vulgarity exists also in wording, through the mention of things outside refined society,
as with a word beginning with ya in the description of the festival of love.
Or, because of the manner of joining words, or again because of the sentence meaning,

children.text: duṣpratītikaraṃ grāmyaṃ yathā yā bhavataḥ priyā ||
children.translated_text: what produces a bad apprehension is vulgar, as in, 'she who is dear to you.'

children.text: kharaṃ prahṛtya viśrāntaḥ puruṣo vīryavān iti
children.translated_text: 'Having struck the ass and rested, the man is powerful.'

children.text: evamādi na śaṃsanti mārgayor ubhayor api ||
children.translated_text: Things of this sort are not approved in either of the two styles.
Words such as 'sister' and 'holy lady' are everywhere accepted.
Sweetness has been distinguished; delicacy is now stated.
Here, what is mostly made of non-harsh syllables is approved as delicate.
But the fault of looseness in composition has been shown in what is entirely soft.
'Spreading out their tail-feathers in circles, with throats sweet in song,
peacocks dance at the time when the clouds are massed.'
Here the meaning is not vigorous, nor is the ornament of that kind;
yet by delicacy alone this climbs into the minds of good people.

children.text: dīptam ity aparair bhūmnā kṛcchrodyam api badhyate
children.translated_text: By others, what is difficult to pronounce may even be composed abundantly as 'brilliant',

children.text: nyakṣeṇa kṣayitaḥ pakṣaḥ kṣatriyāṇāṃ kṣaṇād iti ||
children.translated_text: as in, 'by a small-eyed one the side of the kṣatriyas was destroyed in a moment.'
Clarity of meaning is the absence of needing to be led to the meaning: 'by Hari the earth was raised
from the ocean red with the blood of serpents crushed by his hooves.'
'The earth was raised by the great boar from the red ocean.'
When only this much is stated, the serpent-blood has to be inferred.

children.text: nedṛśaṃ bahu manyate mārgayor ubhayor api
children.translated_text: Neither of the two styles esteems such a thing highly;
for an apprehension that transgresses the rule of words is not beautiful.

children.text: utkarṣavān guṇaḥ kaścid yasminn ukte pratīyate
children.translated_text: When some excellent quality is understood once it has been stated,
that is called elevation; by it the path of poetry is made well-supported.

children.text: arthināṃ kṛpaṇā dṛṣṭis tvanmukhe patitā sakṛt
children.translated_text: The wretched gaze of petitioners, having once fallen on your face,

children.text: tadavasthā punar deva nānyasya mukham īkṣate ||
children.translated_text: In that condition, however, O king, she looks upon no other face.

children.text: iti tyāgasya vākye 'sminn utkarṣaḥ sādhu lakṣyate
children.translated_text: In this utterance of <s>Tyāga</s>, excellence is clearly observed.
By this same method, in other cases too, the same principle should be inferred.

children.text: ślāghyair viśeṣaṇair yuktam udāraṃ kaiścid iṣyate
children.translated_text: Some hold that what is joined with praiseworthy epithets is udāra (noble, elevated),
as in expressions such as playing-lotuses, pleasure-lakes, golden armlets, and the like.
Ojas (vigor) is abundance of compounds; this is the very life of prose.
Even in verse, for those who are not southerners, this alone is the chief resource.
Through mixtures of many and few heavy and light syllables,
that ojas is seen in high and low varieties in ākhyāyikās and similar works.
The western quarter, with a couch made of all the sun's rays flung upon the mountain of sunset,
seems like a woman with a lovely reddish garment resting on her full breasts.

children.text: iti padye 'pi paurastyā badhnanty ojasvinīr giraḥ
children.translated_text: Thus even in verse the eastern poets compose vigorous speech.

children.text: anye tv anākulaṃ hṛdyam icchanty ojo girāṃ yathā ||
children.translated_text: Others, however, desire an ojas in speech that is unconfused and pleasing, as follows:
With the garment of twilight's glow clinging to the slope of her breasts,

children.text: kasya kāmāturaṃ ceto vāruṇī na kariṣyati ||
children.translated_text: whose love-stricken mind will the western quarter not make?
Kānta (charming) expression is charming to all the world because it does not transgress ordinary meaning.
And that is seen both in statements of fact and in descriptions.

children.text: gṛhāṇi nāma tāny eva taporāśir bhavādṛśaḥ
children.translated_text: Those houses alone are truly houses which a mass of austerity such as you
honors with the purifying dust of his feet.
O flawless-limbed woman, for these two breasts of yours as they swell,
the space between your vine-like arms is not sufficient.
Thus, when enriched by a specific statement, this very plausible expression
becomes charming to everyone because it follows the course of worldly life.
When the intended meaning is ascribed excessively, as if beyond the world,

children.text: yo 'rthas tenāti tuṣyanti vidagdhā netare janāḥ ||
children.translated_text: the learned are greatly pleased by it, but other people are not.
From today our house is worthy of worship like a god's shrine,
for all its sin has been washed away by the fall of dust from your feet.
Without reflection, the creator made the sky too small,
since this swelling of your breasts was to become such as it is.

children.text: idam atyuktir ity uktam etad gauḍopalālitam
children.translated_text: This has been called atyukti (hyperbolic overstatement); it is cherished by the Gauḍas.

children.text: prasthānaṃ prākpraṇītaṃ tu sāram anyasya vartmanaḥ ||
children.translated_text: But the method previously set forth is the essence of the other path.
Where, with regard for the limits of the world, the property of one thing

children.text: samyag ādhīyate yatra sa samādhiḥ smṛto yathā ||
children.translated_text: is properly placed upon another, that is remembered as samādhi (transferred attribution), as follows:
The night-lotuses close their eyes, and the day-lotuses open theirs;
through the superimposition of the action of eyes, speech denoting that action has been obtained.
Words such as spat out, disgorged, and vomited, depending on secondary usage,
are extremely beautiful in one context, but enter the sphere of vulgarity in another.
The lotuses, having drunk the fiery drops spat out by the sun's rays,
seem to vomit them again through their mouths, with reddish pollen disgorged.

children.text: iti hṛdyam ahṛdyaṃ tu niḥṣṭhīvati vadhūr iti
children.translated_text: So this is pleasing; but 'the bride spits' is displeasing.

children.text: yugapan naikadharmāṇām adhyāsaś ca smṛto yathā ||
children.translated_text: The simultaneous superimposition of many properties is also remembered as samādhi, as follows:
Wearied by the heavy burden of their wombs, the rows of clouds, rumbling,
lie down on the lap of the mountain slope.
Lying on a lap, a female friend's rumbling, heaviness, and fatigue:
these many properties of a pregnant woman are shown here.

children.text: tad etat kāvyasarvasvaṃ samādhir nāma yo guṇaḥ
children.translated_text: Therefore this quality called samādhi is the whole treasure of poetry;
the entire caravan of poets follows that one quality.
Thus the two paths have been distinguished by defining their nature.

children.text: tadbhedās tu na śakyante vaktuṃ pratikavi sthitāḥ ||
children.translated_text: But their subdivisions cannot be stated, since they are established differently in each poet.
There is a great difference in the sweetness of sugarcane, milk, molasses, and the like,

children.text: tathāpi na tad ākhyātuṃ sarasvatyāpi śakyate ||
children.translated_text: and yet even <s>Sarasvatī</s> could not describe it.

children.text: naisargikī ca pratibhā śrutaṃ ca bahu nirmalam
children.translated_text: Natural genius, much spotless learning,
and tireless application are the cause of the wealth of poetry.

children.text: na vidyate yady api pūrvavāsanāguṇānubandhi pratibhānam adbhutam
children.translated_text: Even if there is no wondrous poetic genius connected with impressions from a former life,

children.text: śrutena yatnena ca vāg upāsitā dhruvaṃ karoty eva kamapy anugraham ||
children.translated_text: speech, when cultivated through learning and effort, surely grants some favor.

children.text: tadastatandrair aniśaṃ sarasvatī śramād upāsyā khalu kīrtim īpsubhiḥ
children.translated_text: Therefore <s>Sarasvatī</s> must indeed be worshiped tirelessly and constantly by those who desire fame through labor.

children.text: kṛśe kavitve 'pi janāḥ kṛtaśramāḥ vidagdhagoṣṭhīṣu vihartum īśate ||
children.translated_text: People who have worked hard, even if their poetry is slight, are able to move among assemblies of the learned.
The properties that produce the beauty of poetry are called alaṃkāras (figures of speech).

children.text: te cādyāpi vikalpyante kas tān kārtsnyena vakṣyati ||
children.translated_text: They are still being variously distinguished even today; who could state them completely?
But the seed of these distinctions has been shown by earlier teachers;
this effort of ours is only to refine that very seed.
Some figures have already been mentioned before for the sake of dividing the paths.
Now the other common class of alaṃkāras is displayed.
Natural description, simile, metaphor, lamp-like linkage, repetition,
objection, statement of a different point, contrast, and imaginative causation;
condensation, excess, poetic fancy, cause, subtlety, a slight figure, sequence,
the affectionate, the sentiment-filled, the forceful, indirect expression, and the composed;
the elevated, denial, punning, distinctions, equal conjunction,
contradiction, irrelevant praise, disguised praise, and illustration;
joint statement, exchange, blessing, mixture, and then the anticipatory figure:
these figures of speech were shown by the earlier sages.
Directly revealing the form of things in their various states,

children.text: svabhāvoktiś ca jātiś cety ādyā sālaṃkṛtir yathā ||
children.translated_text: svabhāvokti (natural description), also called jāti, is the first figure, as follows:
With beaks reddish and curved, with wings green and soft,
and with necks marked by three-colored streaks, these parrots have sweet voices.
With his eyes rolling and his throat filled with a soft cooing sound,
the dove circles about, desiring to make love, and kisses his beloved.
Raising horripilation on the limbs and producing delight in the mind,
and causing the eyes to close, this touch of the beloved takes effect.
With blackness at his throat, with a skull in his hand, and with the moon as his crest-jewel,
<s>Vṛṣadhvaja</s>, <s>Śiva</s>, appeared with matted locks glossy and copper-red.
Such is the description of class, action, quality, substance, and nature.

children.text: śāstreṣvasyaiva sāmrājyaṃ kāvyeṣv apy etad īpsitam ||
children.translated_text: In the śāstras (technical treatises) this alone has sovereignty, and in kāvya (poetry) too this is desired.
Wherever some similarity, in whatever manner, is perceived as having arisen,

children.text: upamā nāma sā tasyāḥ prapañco 'yaṃ nidarśyate ||
children.translated_text: that is called upamā (simile); its elaboration is now illustrated.
"O innocent girl, your palm is reddish like a lotus."
This is direct dharmopamā, because a shared property is explicitly shown.

children.text: rājīvam iva te vaktraṃ netre nīlotpale iva
children.translated_text: "Your face is like a lotus, and your eyes are like blue lotuses."
This is vastūpamā, where a single property is understood; it is just that kind.
"The lotus became open like your face."
Because of the reversal of what is commonly established, this is called viparyāsopamā.

children.text: tavānanam ivāmbhojam ambhojam iva te mukham
children.translated_text: "Your face is like a lotus; the lotus is like your face."
This is anyonyopamā, declaring mutual excellence.
"Your face is equal only to a lotus and to nothing else."
Because similarity with anything else is excluded, this is niyamopamā.

children.text: padmaṃ tāvat tavānveti mukham anyac ca tādṛśam
children.translated_text: "A lotus, at least, resembles your face; and if there is anything else like it,

children.text: asti ced astu tatkārīty asāv aniyamopamā ||
children.translated_text: let that too do so." This is aniyamopamā.
There is also samuccayopamā, as in: "Not by beauty alone does your face
resemble the moon, but also by the action called giving delight."

children.text: tvayyeva tvanmukhaṃ dṛṣṭaṃ dṛśyate divi candramāḥ
children.translated_text: "Your face is seen only in you; the moon is seen in the sky.
Only this much is the difference, nothing else." This is atiśayopamā.

children.text: mayy evāsyā mukhaśrīr ity alam indor vikatthanaiḥ
children.translated_text: "This beauty of her face is in me alone"; enough of the moon's boasting,

children.text: padme 'pi sā yad asty evety asāvutprekṣitopamā ||
children.translated_text: for it certainly exists in the lotus too. This is utprekṣitopamā.

children.text: yadi kiṃcid bhavet padmaṃ subhru vibhrāntalocanam
children.translated_text: "O fair-browed one, if there should be any lotus with wandering eyes,

children.text: tat te mukhaśriyaṃ dhattām ity asāvadbhutopamā ||
children.translated_text: then let it bear the beauty of your face." This is adbhutopamā.
"O slender-limbed one, imagining your face to be the moon, because I long for your face,

children.text: indum apy anudhāvāmīty eṣā mohopamā smṛtā ||
children.translated_text: I pursue even the moon." This is remembered as mohopamā.

children.text: kiṃ padmam antarbhrāntāli kiṃ te lolekṣaṇaṃ mukham
children.translated_text: "Is it a lotus with bees roaming inside, or is it your face with restless eyes?
My mind wavers." This is saṃśayopamā.
"The radiance of a lotus, which is subdued by the moon, does not put the moon to shame;

children.text: atas tvanmukham evedam ity asau nirṇayopamā ||
children.translated_text: therefore this is surely your face." This is nirṇayopamā.
"Rivalling the cool-rayed moon, lovely, and fragrant too,

children.text: ambhojam iva te vaktram iti śleṣopamā smṛtā ||
children.translated_text: your face is like a lotus." This is known as śleṣopamā.
Because it is denoted by words of the same form, that is samānopamā, as in:
"O girl, this garden-garland is beautiful with a grove of sāla trees."

children.text: padmaṃ bahurajaś candraḥ kṣayī tābhyāṃ tavānanam
children.translated_text: "The lotus has much dust, and the moon wanes; compared with both, your face,

children.text: samānam api sotsekam iti nindopamā smṛtā ||
children.translated_text: though similar, is superior." This is remembered as nindopamā.
"The lotus is the source even of <s>Brahmā</s>, and the moon is borne on <s>Śambhu</s>'s head;
those two are equal to your face." This is called praśaṃsopamā.

children.text: candreṇa tvanmukhaṃ tulyam ity ācikhyāsu me manaḥ
children.translated_text: "My mind wishes to say that your face is equal to the moon;

children.text: sa guṇo vāstu doṣo vety ācikhyāsopamāṃ viduḥ ||
children.translated_text: whether that is a merit or a fault, let it be." They know this as ācikhyāsopamā.
"A hundred-petalled lotus, the autumn moon, and your face: these three
are mutually opposed." That is considered virodhopamā.

children.text: na jātu śaktir indos te mukhena pratigarjitum
children.translated_text: "The moon never has the power to contend with your face,
because it is spotted and dull." This is pratiṣedhopamā.
"Your face is marked with deer-eyes; the moon is marked only by a deer.
Even so, it is merely equal, not superior." This is caṭūpamā.

children.text: na padmaṃ mukham evedaṃ na bhṛṅgau cakṣuṣī ime
children.translated_text: "This is not a lotus; it is truly a face. These are not two bees; they are eyes."
Because the resemblance is very clear, this is tattvākhyānopamā.
"Having surpassed the beauty of the moon and the lotus, your face
became equal only to itself." This is asādhāraṇopamā.
"The essence of the splendor of all lotuses seems to have been gathered somewhere;
your face shines so." They know that as abhūtopamā.

children.text: candrabimbād iva viṣaṃ candanād iva pāvakaḥ
children.translated_text: "Like poison from the disk of the moon, like fire from sandalwood,

children.text: paruṣā vāg ito vaktrād ity asaṃbhāvitopamā ||
children.translated_text: harsh speech comes from this face." This is asaṃbhāvitopamā.
"Your touch is cool like sandal-water, moonbeams, moonstone, and the like."
By indicating excess, this is bahūpamā.
"O slender-limbed one, your face seems carved from the moon's disk,

children.text: tava tanvaṅgi vadanam ity asau vikriyopamā ||
children.translated_text: or drawn out from the heart of a lotus." This is vikriyopamā.

children.text: pūṣṇy ātapa ivāhnīva pūṣā vyomnīva vāsaraḥ
children.translated_text: "As heat is in the sun, as the sun is in the day, as the day is in the sky,

children.text: vikramas tvayy adhāl lakṣmīm iti mālopamā matā ||
children.translated_text: so valor has placed splendor in you." This is considered mālopamā.
If some sentence-meaning is compared precisely with a sentence-meaning,
because it may have one or many words expressing comparison, vākyārthopamā is of two kinds.
"Your face, with restless eyes and the flash of teeth appearing,
shines like a lotus with bees circling and filaments indistinctly seen."

children.text: nalinyā iva tanvaṅgyās tasyāḥ padmam ivānanam
children.translated_text: "Like a lotus belonging to a lotus-bed was the face of that slender woman;
I, like a honey-bee, enjoyed it by drinking and drinking."
When, after introducing some object, one sets down another that has the same property as it,
there is the apprehension of similarity: this is prativastūpamā, as in:
"Even now, among kings being born, there is not one like you;

children.text: nanu dvitīyo nāsty eva pārijātasya pādapaḥ ||
children.translated_text: indeed there is no second tree of the pārijāta."
Having made an inferior thing equal to a superior one in the performance of a single action,

children.text: yad bruvanti smṛtā seyaṃ tulyayogopamā yathā ||
children.translated_text: What they call thus is known as the simile of equal connection, as follows:

children.text: divo jāgarti rakṣāyai pulomārir bhuvo bhavān
children.translated_text: For the protection of heaven <s>Pulomāri</s> keeps watch; for the protection of earth, you do, sir.

children.text: asurās tena hanyante sāvalepās tvayā nṛpāḥ ||
children.translated_text: By him the arrogant <s>asuras</s> are slain; by you, kings are slain.

children.text: kāntyā candramasaṃ dhāmnā sūryaṃ dhairyeṇa cārṇavam
children.translated_text: In beauty you imitate the moon, in splendor the sun, and in steadiness the ocean,
O king: this is regarded as a causal simile.

children.text: na liṅgavacane bhinne na hīnādhikatāpi vā
children.translated_text: Difference in gender or number, nor even inferiority or superiority,
is enough to spoil a simile where there is no offence to the wise.

children.text: strīva gacchati ṣaṇḍho 'yaṃ vakty eṣā strī pumān iva
children.translated_text: "This eunuch walks like a woman"; "this woman speaks like a man";

children.text: prāṇā iva priyo 'yam me vidyā dhanam ivārjitam ||
children.translated_text: "he is dear to me like life-breaths"; "learning is like wealth acquired."
Like you, O protector of the earth, the king of the gods shines forth;

children.text: alam aṃśumataḥ kakṣām āroḍhuṃ tejasā nṛpaḥ ||
children.translated_text: a king is able by his brilliance to climb into the sphere of the sun.

children.text: ity evam ādau saubhāgyaṃ na jahāty eva jātucit
children.translated_text: In such examples and the like, charm never departs at all.

children.text: asty eva kvacid udvegaḥ prayoge vāgvidāṃ yathā ||
children.translated_text: Yet in some usage there is offence for those who know speech, as follows:
"The moon is white like a female goose"; "the stainless sky is like lakes";

children.text: bhartṛbhakto bhaṭaḥ śveva khadyoto bhāti bhānuvat ||
children.translated_text: "a soldier devoted to his lord is like a dog"; "a firefly shines like the sun."

children.text: īdṛśaṃ varjyate sadbhiḥ kāraṇaṃ tatra cintyatām
children.translated_text: Such a thing is avoided by good poets; the reason there
should be considered by the discerning themselves for the examination of merits and faults.
The words <s>iva</s>, <s>vat</s>, <s>vā</s>, and <s>yathā</s>; words such as <s>samāna</s>, <s>nibha</s>, and <s>saṃnibha</s>;
<s>tulya</s>, <s>saṃkāśa</s>, <s>nikāśa</s>, <s>prakāśa</s>, and <s>pratirūpaka</s>;
<s>pratipakṣa</s>, <s>pratidvaṃdvin</s>, <s>pratyanīka</s>, and <s>virodhin</s>;
<s>sadṛk</s>, <s>sadṛśa</s>, <s>saṃvādin</s>, <s>sajātīya</s>, and <s>anuvādin</s>;
<s>pratibimba</s>, <s>praticchanda</s>, <s>sarūpa</s>, <s>sama</s>, and <s>saṃmita</s>;
<s>salakṣaṇa</s>, <s>sadṛkṣa</s>, <s>ābhā</s>, <s>sapakṣa</s>, <s>upamita</s>, and <s>upamā</s>;
terms beginning with <s>kalpa</s>, <s>deśīya</s>, and <s>deśya</s>, and also <s>prakhya</s> and <s>pratinidhi</s>;
the words <s>savarṇa</s> and <s>tulā</s>, and others that state a sense of no lessness;
and the compound, namely the <s>bahuvrīhi</s>, in expressions such as "moon-faced";
"competes," "surpasses," "hates," "injures," "roars back against,"
"abuses," "disdains," "maltreats," "blames,"
"mocks," "rivals," "laughs at," "envies," and "resents";

children.text: tasya muṣṇāti saubhāgyaṃ tasya kāntiṃ vilumpati
children.translated_text: "steals his good fortune," "plunders his beauty,"
"quarrels with him," "mounts the balance with him,"

children.text: tatpadavyām padaṃ dhatte tasya kakṣāṃ vigāhate
children.translated_text: "sets foot in his track," "enters his sphere,"
"follows him," "clings to him," "has his character," "denies him,"
and "imitates him": these are words that express similarity.
They have been taught in simile, giving ease to the minds of poets.
A simile in which the difference has disappeared is called <s>rūpaka</s> (metaphor),
as in "arm-creepers," "hand-lotuses," and "foot-sprouts."
The fingers were shoots, the rays of the nails were flowers;

children.text: bāhū late vasantaśrīs tvaṃ naḥ pratyakṣacāriṇī ||
children.translated_text: the arms were creepers; you are spring's beauty moving visibly before us.
This is called uncompounded; when compounded, it is the preceding kind of metaphor.
"The smile is moonlight of the face-moon": this is a metaphor both compounded and uncompounded.
Your lotus foot, with its row of coppery finger-petals and filaments that are the gleams of the nails,
is borne on their heads by kings.
Since petalhood and the rest are superimposed on the toes and so on, and lotushood on the foot,
through placement in the proper locations for them, this is a complete metaphor.
Suddenly, O passionate woman, your face, with lower lip as a trembling shoot,
bears clusters of pearl-bright drops of sweat.
By making the sweat-drops into clusters and the lip into a shoot,
but not otherwise altering the face here, it is therefore a metaphor of the parts.
With playful brow, flowing sweat-water, and reddened eyes,
this face-lotus reveals the condition of intoxication.
Without transforming the parts of the face, the face itself here
has been made into a lotus; therefore this is a metaphor of the whole.
By your face, with cheeks reddened by passion and eyes as red lotuses,

children.text: mukhena mugdhaḥ so 'py eṣa jano rāgamayaḥ kṛtaḥ ||
children.translated_text: even this innocent person has been made full of passion.
This is a one-part metaphor, and likewise there are metaphors beginning with two parts.
Here the presence or absence of connection among the represented parts creates the distinction.
"This face is bright with smile-flowers and has restless eyes as bees":
because of the association of flowers and bees, this is a connected metaphor.
"This face has moist smile-moonlight and glossy eye-lotuses":
because moonlight and lotuses are not connected, it is called an unconnected metaphor.
Because the principal object and its parts may be represented, or may rest on representation and non-representation,

children.text: rūpakaṃ viṣamaṃ nāma lalitaṃ jāyate yathā ||
children.translated_text: there arises a charming metaphor called mixed, as follows:
With your face-moon, whose cheeks are reddened by passion
and whose brow-creeper dances, <s>Manmatha</s> is fully able to crush the three worlds.
The foot of <s>Hari</s>, with the water-cloth of <s>Jahnukanyā</s> clinging to its head,
triumphs as the festival-banner of joy for the gods, who are fearless of the <s>asuras</s>.
Since such is the form of the banner together with its full set of qualifiers,
and that is attributed to the foot, this is a metaphor with qualifiers.

children.text: na mīlayati padmāni na nabho 'py avagāhate
children.translated_text: It does not close lotuses, nor does it enter the sky;
your face-moon is fit only to take away my life-breaths.
Because here the non-performance of moon-actions and the performance of another action

children.text: atra saṃdarśyate yasmād viruddhaṃ nāma rūpakam ||
children.translated_text: are shown, it is called a contrary metaphor.
By depth you are the ocean; by weightiness you are a mountain;

children.text: kāmadatvāc ca lokānām asi tvaṃ kalpapādapaḥ ||
children.translated_text: and because you grant people's desires, you are the wish-fulfilling tree.
Because here, through causes beginning with depth,

children.text: kalpadrumaś ca kriyate tad idaṃ heturūpakam ||
children.translated_text: the ocean, the mountain, and the wish-fulfilling tree are produced, this is a causal metaphor.
For the enjoyment of royal swans, with fragrance desired by bees,
friend, this face-lotus of yours: this is a punned metaphor.
The desired form, through the showing of similarity and dissimilarity between secondary and primary usage,
is the twofold rūpaka (metaphor) called simile-metaphor and contrast-metaphor, as follows:
This face-moon of yours, reddish in hue from passion,
roars back at the moon, whose rising redness is armed for battle.
The moon is drunk by the gods, but your face-moon is drunk by me;
that one is sometimes not full, while this one has a full disk forever.
Thus, lovely one, the moon-ness of the face-moon,

children.text: na te sundari saṃvādīty etad ākṣeparūpakam ||
children.translated_text: since it torments another, does not correspond to you: this is ākṣepa-rūpaka (metaphor by objection).

children.text: mukhendur api te caṇḍi māṃ nirdahati nirdayam
children.translated_text: Even your face-moon, fierce lady, burns me mercilessly;
it is only because of the fault of my own fortune: that is samādhāna-rūpaka (metaphor by resolution).
In this theater of your lotus-face, the dancing girl that is the creeper of your eyebrow
performs a graceful dance of play: this is the charming rūpaka-rūpaka (metaphor upon metaphor).

children.text: naitan mukham idaṃ padmaṃ na netre bhramarāv imau
children.translated_text: This is not a face, it is a lotus; these two eyes are not bees;

children.text: etāni kesarāṇy eva naitā dantārciṣas tava ||
children.translated_text: these indeed are filaments, not the rays of your teeth.
Since face-ness and the rest are removed, and the representation is made by lotus-ness and the rest,
with the excellence of the qualities brought to light, that is apahnava-rūpaka (metaphor by denial).
Therefore there is no limit to the varieties of metaphor and simile;
only a mere indication has been shown by the wise; what has not been stated should be inferred.
When a word denoting class, action, quality, or substance, occurring in one place,

children.text: sarvavākyopakāraś cet tad āhur dīpakaṃ yathā ||
children.translated_text: assists the whole sentence, they call that dīpaka (lamp-like linkage), as follows:

children.text: pavano dakṣiṇaḥ parṇaṃ jīrṇaṃ harati vīrudhāṃ
children.translated_text: The southern wind carries away the withered leaf of the creepers;
that very wind serves to break the pride of women whose limbs are bowed down.
Your elephants move in gardens bordered by the shores of the four oceans,
and your virtues, white as jasmine, move in the bowers of the circle-mountain.
Dark are the quarters with rows of rainy-season clouds,
and the lands are delicate with lines of fresh grass.
By <s>Viṣṇu</s>, standing in his stride, the glories of the demons

children.text: kvāpi nītāḥ kuto 'py āsann ānītā daivatarddhayaḥ ||
children.translated_text: were taken away somewhere, and the prosperities of the gods were brought from somewhere.

children.text: ity ādidīpakāny uktāny evaṃ madhyāntayor api
children.translated_text: Such are initial dīpakas. In the same way, in the middle and at the end
of sentences we shall show some examples of them, as follows:
Peacocks dance on the slopes of nicula trees and sing,
and they fasten glances pregnant with tears of joy upon the clouds.

children.text: mando gandhavahaḥ kṣāro vahnir induś ca jāyate
children.translated_text: The fragrant wind becomes sluggish, briny; fire and the moon become
a fall of powdered sandal and a fall of weapons for travelers abroad.
The water poured out by the clouds is the family of the household peacocks,

children.text: calaṃ ca taḍitāṃ dāma balaṃ kusumadhanvanaḥ ||
children.translated_text: the garland of lightning is restless, and the strength of <s>Kusumadhanvan</s> is strong.
By you a blue lotus was placed at the ear, by <s>Smara</s> a weapon on his bow,

children.text: mayāpi maraṇe cetas trayam etat samaṃ kṛtam ||
children.translated_text: and by me my mind was placed on death: these three were done alike.

children.text: śuklaḥ śvetārciṣo vṛddhyai pakṣaḥ pañcaśarasya saḥ
children.translated_text: The bright fortnight, belonging to the white-rayed moon, is for the increase of the five-arrowed god;

children.text: sa ca rāgasya rāgo 'pi yūnāṃ ratyutsavaśriyaḥ ||
children.translated_text: and he is for passion, and passion too is for the splendor of young men's festival of love.
Although this also has the character of dīpaka, because each earlier sentence depends on the previous one
and a garland of sentences is employed, it is considered mālā-dīpaka (garland dīpaka).
The clouds increase the arrogance of <s>Anaṅga</s>,
but they diminish that of the heat, with drops of water shaken loose by the wind.
Here, through the word 'arrogance' and the word 'clouds',

children.text: kriye viruddhe saṃyukte tad viruddhārthaṃ dīpakam ||
children.translated_text: two opposed actions are joined; that is dīpaka with opposed meanings.

children.text: haraty ābhogam āśānāṃ gṛhṇāti jyotiṣāṃ gaṇam
children.translated_text: It takes away the expanse of the quarters, seizes the multitude of stars,

children.text: ādatte cādya me prāṇān asau jaladharāvalī ||
children.translated_text: and today takes even my life, this row of rainclouds.
Because many words are taken up, one single action alone is illuminated here
with respect to the row of rainclouds; therefore it is single-meaning dīpaka.
Pleasant with fragrant winds, lofty, dark in luster like tamāla trees,

children.text: divi bhramanti jīmūtā bhuvi caite mataṃgajāḥ ||
children.translated_text: clouds wander in the sky, and these elephants wander on the earth.

children.text: atra dharmair abhinnānām abhrāṇāṃ dantināṃ tathā
children.translated_text: Here, for clouds and elephants, which are not different with respect to their properties,
there is connection only through wandering; thus it is śliṣṭārtha-dīpaka (dīpaka with a joined meaning).
In this very manner, with regard to dīpaka,
the wise should understand the remaining varieties as well.
Repetition of meaning, repetition of words, and repetition of both:
three figures are accepted in the place of dīpaka, as follows:
The kadamba trees blossom, the kuṭaja trees burst open,

children.text: unmīlanti ca kandalyo dalanti kakubhāni ca ||
children.translated_text: the plantain shoots open their eyes, and the kakubha trees split forth.
The garland of clouds excites the flock of peacocks with longing,
and <s>Makaradhvaja</s> likewise excites the minds of young men with longing.

children.text: jitvā viśvaṃ bhavān atra viharaty avarodhanaiḥ
children.translated_text: Having conquered the world, you sport here with the women of your inner apartments;

children.text: viharaty apsarobhis te ripuvargo divaṃ gataḥ ||
children.translated_text: your enemy host, gone to heaven, sports with the celestial nymphs.
A statement of prohibition is ākṣepa (objection), threefold with reference to the three times;
and again, because the things objected to are endless in their divisions, it is endless.
<s>Anaṅga</s> conquered the world with five flower-arrows:
this is impossible; or else the powers of things are wondrous.
Here the thought that <s>Anaṅga</s>'s conquest is impossible, though it had arisen through the force of a reason,

children.text: pravṛttaiva yad ākṣiptā vṛttākṣepaḥ sa īdṛśaḥ ||
children.translated_text: is itself objected to; such is past ākṣepa.
Why, sweet-voiced one, do you place a blue lotus at your ear?

children.text: kim apāṅgam aparyāptam asmin karmaṇi manyase ||
children.translated_text: Do you think your sidelong glance is insufficient for this task?
This is present ākṣepa; while she is placing a dark lotus
at her ear, a certain woman is restrained in this way by her beloved, skilled in flattery.

children.text: satyaṃ bravīmi na tvaṃ māṃ draṣṭuṃ vallabha lapsyase
children.translated_text: I speak the truth: beloved, you will not be able to look at me
with an eye reddened by lac transferred from kissing another woman.
This is future ākṣepa; a proud woman restrained him beforehand,
thinking, 'some offense of his may occur at some time in the future.'

children.text: tava tanvaṅgi mithyaiva rūḍham aṅgeṣu mārdavam
children.translated_text: O slender-limbed one, the softness grown upon your limbs is surely false;

children.text: yadi satyaṃ mṛdūny eva kim akāṇḍe rujanti mām ||
children.translated_text: if they truly are soft, why do they wound me so suddenly?
This is dharmākṣepa (objection to a property): the softness of the woman’s body is objected to,
because the lover objects to it here through an action opposed to that very property.

children.text: sundarī sā bhavaty evaṃ vivekaḥ kena jāyate
children.translated_text: In this way she is beautiful. How can discrimination arise?

children.text: prabhāmātraṃ hi taralaṃ dṛśyate na tadāśrayaḥ ||
children.translated_text: For only a wavering radiance is seen, not its support.
This is dharmyākṣepa (objection to the possessor of a property): the subject possessing the property called radiance is objected to,
when someone wishing to express an exceedingly wondrous beauty grants the form itself only indirectly.
Your eyes are reddened; the tender shoot of your lower lip is quivering;

children.text: bhruvau ca bhugne na tathāpy aduṣṭasyāsti me bhayam ||
children.translated_text: your brows are bent, and yet I, innocent as I am, feel no fear.

children.text: sa eṣa kāraṇākṣepaḥ pradhānaṃ kāraṇaṃ bhiyaḥ
children.translated_text: This is kāraṇākṣepa (objection to the cause), where the chief cause of fear,
one’s own offense, is denied by the very clever beloved.
My dearest is far away; this arrival of the rainy season has come;

children.text: dṛṣṭāś ca phullā niculā na mṛtā cāsmi kiṃ nv idam ||
children.translated_text: the blossoming niculas have been seen, and yet I am not dead. What can this be?
That is kāryākṣepa (objection to the effect), because the effect, namely death, is set aside,
after its dreadful cause, the arrival of the rainy season, has been presented.

children.text: na ciraṃ mama tāpāya tava yātrā bhaviṣyati
children.translated_text: Your journey will not long be a source of torment to me;

children.text: yadi yāsyasi yātavyam alam āśaṅkayātra te ||
children.translated_text: if you will go, you must go. Enough of your anxiety here.
In this way, through the guise of permission itself, the lover’s going is objected to;
because she thereby suggests her death, it is called anujñākṣepa (objection through permission).

children.text: dhanaṃ ca bahu labhyaṃ te sukhaṃ kṣemaṃ ca vartmani
children.translated_text: You will obtain much wealth, and there will be ease and safety on the road;

children.text: na ca me prāṇasaṃdehas tathāpi priya mā sma gāḥ ||
children.translated_text: nor is there any doubt about my life. Even so, dear one, do not go.
When the beloved states the reasons connected with the beloved’s journey,
and blocks it precisely by making them abundant, that is called prabhutvākṣepa (objection through abundance).
My hope of living is strong; my hope for wealth is weak.

children.text: gaccha vā tiṣṭha vā kānta svavasthā tu niveditā ||
children.translated_text: Go, or stay, beloved: my condition has merely been reported.
This is anādarākṣepa (objection through disregard), where speech resembling disregard
is used here by a passionate woman while she restrains her beloved’s departure.

children.text: gaccha gacchasi cet kānta panthānaḥ santu te śivāḥ
children.translated_text: Go, if you are going, beloved; may the roads be auspicious for you.

children.text: mamāpi janma tatraiva bhūyād yatra gato bhavān ||
children.translated_text: May my own birth also be there, wherever you have gone.
This is āśīrvacanākṣepa (objection through blessing), when by way of a blessing
the beloved’s journey is forbidden while she merely suggests her own state.

children.text: yadi satyaiva yātrā te kāpy anyā mṛgyatāṃ tvayā
children.translated_text: If your journey is indeed certain, then some other woman should be sought by you;
for today itself I am held fast by death, which is waiting for an opening.
This is paruṣākṣepa (harsh objection), since, preceded by harsh syllables,
the beloved’s departure is objected to by a woman whose love has been wounded.

children.text: gantā ced gaccha tūrṇaṃ te karṇau yānti purā ravāḥ
children.translated_text: If you are going, go quickly, before sounds reach your ears,
uttered from the mouths of my afflicted friends and obstructing your departure.
This is precisely sācivyākṣepa (objection through assistance), because here
the beloved’s departure is forbidden by an intensely attached woman even while she seems to help it.
I wish to say, ‘Go,’ my dear, since I seek what is dear to you;

children.text: nirgacchati mukhād vāṇī mā gā iti karomi kim ||
children.translated_text: but from my mouth comes the utterance, ‘Do not go.’ What am I to do?
That is yatnākṣepa (objection to an effort), because an effort made toward an undesirable thing
is shown to be useless, since the opposite result arises from it.
When love is angry even at the fluttering of an eyelash, because it obstructs sight for an instant,

children.text: premṇaḥ prayāṇaṃ tvaṃ brūhi mayā tasyeṣṭam iṣyate ||
children.translated_text: you tell me whether departure is dear to it; whatever it desires, I accept.
This is paravaśākṣepa (objection through being under another’s power), because, being subject to love,
she forbids the journey by suggesting the purpose of another power.

children.text: sahiṣye virahaṃ nātha dehy adṛśyāñjanaṃ mama
children.translated_text: I shall endure separation, lord; give me invisible collyrium,

children.text: yad aktanetrāṃ kandarpaḥ prahartā māṃ na paśyati ||
children.translated_text: so that <s>Kandarpa</s>, not seeing me with eyes so anointed, will not strike me.
When an impossible means of preserving life is put forward,

children.text: patyuḥ prasthānam ity āhur upāyākṣepam īdṛśam ||
children.translated_text: and the husband’s departure is thereby obstructed, they call such a case upāyākṣepa (objection through a means).

children.text: pravṛttaiva prayāmīti vāṇī vallabha te mukhāt
children.translated_text: The statement ‘I am going’ has already come forth from your mouth, beloved;
what have I now to do with you, who have little love, even without effort?
This is roṣākṣepa (angry objection), when the departure undertaken by the beloved
is forbidden by an enraged woman whose self-control has been overwhelmed by overflowing affection.
The innocent girl, simply on hearing mention of her beloved’s journey, fainted;

children.text: buddhvā vakti priyaṃ dṛṣṭvā kiṃ cireṇāgato bhavān ||
children.translated_text: then, regaining consciousness and seeing her beloved, she says, ‘Why have you come after so long?’
When the lover’s going is objected to by the fainting that arose at that very moment

children.text: kāntasya kātarākṣyā yan mūrchākṣepaḥ sa īdṛśaḥ ||
children.translated_text: in the timid-eyed woman, that is the kind called mūrchākṣepa (objection through fainting).

children.text: nāghrātaṃ na kṛtaṃ karṇe strībhir madhuni nārpitam
children.translated_text: It has not been smelled, not placed at the ear, not offered by women in wine;
the blue lotus has withered only in the pond-mouths of your enemies.
This is anukrośākṣepa (compassionate objection), since, as if compassionately toward the lotus,
an action proper to it is diverted by showing its pitiable state.
Since the moon of your face truly exists, with the nature of nectar, enemy of lotuses, and moist stars for pupils,

children.text: mukhendau tava satyasmin apareṇa kim indunā ||
children.translated_text: what use is there for another moon?
Thus the face-moon is objected to after displaying qualities
equal to those belonging to the secondary moon; such is śliṣṭākṣepa (objection through double application).

children.text: artho na saṃbhṛtaḥ kaścin na vidyā kācid arcitā
children.translated_text: No wealth at all has been amassed; no learning has been honored;

children.text: na tapaḥ saṃcintaṃ kiṃcid gataṃ ca sakalaṃ vayaḥ ||
children.translated_text: no austerity at all has been undertaken, and the whole of life has passed away.
This is anuśayākṣepa (objection through regret), because, following upon regret,
the cessation of wealth-getting and the like is shown here by one whose life is spent.

children.text: kim ayaṃ śaradambhodaḥ kiṃ vā haṃsakadambakam
children.translated_text: Is this an autumn cloud, or perhaps a flock of geese?

children.text: rutaṃ nūpurasaṃvādi śrūyate tan na toyadaḥ ||
children.translated_text: A cry harmonious with anklets is heard; therefore it is not a raincloud.

children.text: ity ayaṃ saṃśayākṣepaḥ saṃśayo yan nivartyate
children.translated_text: This is saṃśayākṣepa (objection through doubt), because a doubt is removed
by a property common among geese: not being produced from an untouched cloud.

children.text: citram ākrāntaviśvo 'pi vikramas te na tṛpyati
children.translated_text: It is wondrous: although your valor has overrun the whole world, it is not satisfied.

children.text: kadā vā dṛśyate tṛptir udīrṇasya havirbhujaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Or when is satisfaction ever seen in a blazing fire?
This is arthantaraksepa (objection by another meaning): what has been begun is restrained,
because amazement arises here from seeing another thing that has the same property.

children.text: na stūyase narendra tvaṃ dadāsīti kadācana
children.translated_text: You are never praised, O king, with the words, 'you give';

children.text: svam eva matvā gṛhṇanti yatas tvaddhanam arthinaḥ ||
children.translated_text: for petitioners take your wealth as though thinking it their own.
An objection such as this is remembered as hetvaksepa (objection by reason).
By this very indication, the other alternatives too can be inferred.
That should be known as arthantaranyasa (placing of another meaning): after presenting some matter,
there is the placing of another matter capable of establishing it.
Pervading the universe, standing in a particular instance, pierced by double meaning, containing contradiction,
acting improperly, proper in nature, both proper and improper, and reversed:
such and similar divisions of this are observed in usage.
A garland of examples of these is set forth to make their forms clear.
Even the blessed sun and moon, the two eyes of the world,

children.text: paśya gacchata evāstaṃ niyatiḥ kena laṅghyate ||
children.translated_text: behold, go down. By whom can destiny be crossed?
Clouds indeed remove the distress of embodied beings;
is not the attainment of greatness for the quieting of others' suffering?
The breeze from <s>Malaya</s> produces delight in the world.
Surely one endowed with kindness becomes dear to everyone.
This moon gladdens the world, although it is stained.
For a lord of twice-born beings, even with faults, benefits others.
Though the sound of bees comes from throats excited by drinking honey,

children.text: kaṭur bhavati karṇasya kāmināṃ pāpam īdṛśam ||
children.translated_text: it becomes harsh to the ear of lovers: such is sin.
This bed of lotus petals burns my body.
Surely it is fitting that a substitute for fire should have burning as its nature.

children.text: kṣiṇotu kāmaṃ śītāṃśuḥ kiṃ vasanto dunoti mām
children.translated_text: Let the cool-rayed moon torment me if it must; why does spring afflict me?
Surely conduct stained with impurity is improper for one fragrant by nature.

children.text: kumudāny api dāhāya kim ayaṃ kamalākaraḥ
children.translated_text: Why is this mass of lotuses for the burning even of night-lotuses?
For honey, when harsh to those grasped by the moon, would not become pleasant when grasped by the sun.

children.text: śabdopātte pratīte vā sādṛśye vastunor dvayoḥ
children.translated_text: When similarity between two things is expressed by words or understood by implication,

children.text: tatra yad bhedakathanaṃ vyatirekaḥ sa kathyate ||
children.translated_text: the statement of difference there is called vyatireka (contrast).
In courage, beauty, depth, and the like, you are equal to the ocean;

children.text: guṇais tulyo 'si bhedas tu vapuṣaivedṛśena te ||
children.translated_text: but the difference lies in this very body of yours.
This is single vyatireka, because the difference, through a property present in only one of the two,
comes within the range of apprehension though the difference belongs to both.
The ocean and you alike have unbroken limits and are deep;
that one is like collyrium in appearance, while you have the splendor of gold.
This is double vyatireka, because two distinguishing qualities of the two

children.text: kārṣṇyaṃ piśaṅgatā cobhau yat pṛthag darśitāv iha ||
children.translated_text: blackness and tawny-golden color, have both been shown separately here.

children.text: tvaṃ samudraś ca durvārau mahāsattvau satejasau
children.translated_text: You and the ocean are both hard to withstand, of great essence, and full of brilliance.

children.text: ayaṃ tu yuvayor bhedaḥ sa jaḍātmā paṭur bhavān ||
children.translated_text: But this is the difference between you two: it is inert in nature, while you are skillful.

children.text: sa eṣa śleṣarūpatvāt saśleṣa iti gṛhyatām
children.translated_text: Because this has the form of slesa (double meaning), let it be understood as containing slesa.

children.text: sākṣepaś ca sahetuś ca darśyate tad api dvayam ||
children.translated_text: The two further kinds, with objection and with reason, are also shown.

children.text: sthitimān api dhīro 'pi ratnānām ākaro 'pi san
children.translated_text: Though it is stable, though deep, and though an abode of jewels,

children.text: tava kakṣāṃ na yāty eva malino makarālayaḥ ||
children.translated_text: the dark, sea-monster-filled ocean never reaches your rank.
Although <s>Sesa</s> bears the whole earth, together with its mountains, continents, and oceans,
he is inferior to you because he is the lord of serpents.
Such is vyatireka where similarity is taken up by words.
There is also a kind whose similarity is understood by implication; that too is stated.

children.text: tvanmukhaṃ kamalaṃ ceti dvayor apy anayor bhidā
children.translated_text: 'Your face is a lotus': between these two there is difference as well.
The lotus grows in water; your face rests on you.
This pair of your eyes is without play of brows, untouched by the redness of intoxication, and gazelle-eyed;
but that other pair is adorned with those qualities.
In the earlier case there is merely a statement of difference; in this one, superiority is shown.
And another similar vyatireka is next displayed.
Your face and a white lotus are both blooming and sweetly fragrant;

children.text: bhramadbhramaram ambhojaṃ lolanetraṃ mukhaṃ tu te ||
children.translated_text: the lotus has wandering bees, but your face has restless eyes.
This moon is the crest-ornament of the sky; this swan is the ornament of the water.
This sky has a garland of stars; the water has blossoming night-lotuses.
In this example, between sky and water, whose likeness in whiteness and so on is apprehended,
and between the moon and the swan, whose purity is apprehended, a difference has been made.
In the previous example, as if verbally expressed, the similarity in both cases also served as the distinguisher.
There the bees, eyes, and so forth are equivalent; that is similar vyatireka.
Not removable by the sight of jewels, not removable by the rays of the sun,
the darkness born of youth blocks the sight of young men.
This is vyatireka within the same class: this darkness belongs to the class of darkness.

children.text: dṛṣṭirodhitayā tulyaṃ bhinnam anyair adarśi tat ||
children.translated_text: It is equal in blocking sight, but it is shown to differ in other respects.
Where, through the exclusion of a well-known cause, some other cause

children.text: yatra svābhāvikatvaṃ vā vibhāvyaṃ sā vibhāvanā ||
children.translated_text: or naturalness is to be made manifest, that is vibhavana (special imagination).
The world was charming, though the intoxicated kadamba trees had not drunk, and though the sky's cloud-line had not been wiped away,
and though the pure waters had not been made clear.
Your glance is dark though unpainted; your brow is bent though not curved by effort;
and this lip of yours, O beautiful one, is red though not dyed.
That which would be produced by drinking and the like is here said to arise from another cause of intoxication and so on,
or to be causeless; thus there is no contradiction in the intended meaning.
Her face is fragrant by nature; her body is beautiful without artifice.
The moon is an enemy without cause, and <s>Smara</s> is a foe without reason.
Here, by words such as 'by nature,' the cause is directly excluded;

children.text: uktaṃ ca surabhitvādi phalaṃ tat sā vibhāvanā ||
children.translated_text: and the result, such as fragrance, has been stated. That is <s>vibhāvanā</s>.
When some object is intended, and another object similar to it
is stated, because this has the form of condensation, it is accepted as <s>samāsokti</s>.
A bee, drinking honey as it wishes on a fully opened lotus,
look, kisses even a bud whose fragrance has not yet unfolded.
Thus, in the case of a passionate man whose sport of love is bound to a mature woman,
his movement of desire toward some young girl here is suggested.
Although differing only in the qualified subject, there is one kind with similar qualifiers;
there is also another, with qualifiers both different and not different.
Deep-rooted, nourishing suppliants constantly with masses of fruit,
dense in shade: this great tree has been reached by me.
With abundant spread of branches, rich in fruit and flowers,

children.text: socchrayaḥ sthairyavān daivād eṣa labdho mayā drumaḥ ||
children.translated_text: lofty and firm: by fortune this tree has been obtained by me.
In both cases some man is described under the form of a tree;

children.text: sarve sādhāraṇā dharmāḥ pūrvatrānyatra tu dvayam ||
children.translated_text: in the first all qualities are common, but in the other two are different.
Freed from contact with serpents, naturally sweet in its depths,
this ocean, alas, dries up in time.
This is an unprecedented <s>samāsokti</s>, because the previous qualities are negated,
and because it indicates the misfortune of a man who is similar to the ocean.
An intention to express a special quality that oversteps the boundary of ordinary life
is <s>atiśayokti</s>, the highest of ornaments, as follows:
Women going to a tryst, wearing jasmine garlands, with wet sandal over every limb,
and dressed in linen, are not seen in the moonlight.
The abundance of moonlight has been expressed as possessing excellence.
To make clear doubt, exaggeration, and the like, something is illustrated.

children.text: stanayor jaghanasyāpi madhye madhyaṃ priye tava
children.translated_text: Between your breasts and also your hips, beloved, the waist

children.text: asti nāstīti saṃdeho na me 'dyāpi nivartate ||
children.translated_text: whether it exists or does not exist: my doubt has not even today ceased.

children.text: nirṇetuṃ śakyam astīti madhyaṃ tava nitambini
children.translated_text: Your waist can be determined to exist, broad-hipped one,
only because otherwise the position of the weight of your breasts would be impossible.
Ah, king, vast is the belly of the three worlds,

children.text: mātimātum aśakyo 'pi yaśorāśir yad atra te ||
children.translated_text: since the mass of your fame is here, though impossible to measure.
They say that even the other ornaments have one supreme refuge:
this expression, honored by masters of speech, called <s>atiśaya</s>.
Where the mode of existence of something conscious or otherwise, though actually situated one way,

children.text: anyathotprekṣyate yatra tām utprekṣāṃ vidur yathā ||
children.translated_text: is imagined in another way, they know that as <s>utprekṣā</s>, as follows:
An elephant, scorched by the midday sun, enters a lake;
I think he is intent on uprooting the lotuses, the dependents of <s>Mārtaṇḍa</s>.

children.text: snātuṃ pātuṃ bisāny attuṃ kariṇo jalagāhanam
children.translated_text: The elephant's plunging into water is for bathing, drinking, and eating lotus fibers;
yet the poet describes it by supposing, 'it is to exact payment for their enemy.'
'This is the ornament of the ear of my approaching enemy';

children.text: iti karṇotpalaṃ prāyas tava dṛṣṭyā vilaṅghyate ||
children.translated_text: so the blue lotus at your ear is generally overstepped by your glance.
With the rays of a glance falling at the edge of the eye, the lotus

children.text: spṛśyate vā na vety evaṃ kavinotprekṣya varṇyate ||
children.translated_text: is touched or perhaps not: in this way it is described by the poet through supposition.
Darkness seems to smear the limbs; the sky seems to rain collyrium:
this too is mostly endowed with the mark of <s>utprekṣā</s>.
Some people here fall into the mistaken notion of simile because the word 'as if' is heard,
transgressing the authoritative statement that a finite verb is not a standard of comparison.
The status of standard and object of comparison depends upon a shared property;

children.text: limpates tamasaś cāsau dharmaḥ ko 'tra samīkṣyate ||
children.translated_text: but of smearing and of darkness, what property is observed here?

children.text: yadi lepanam eveṣṭaṃ limpatir nāma ko 'paraḥ
children.translated_text: If smearing itself is desired, what other thing, pray, is the verb 'smears'?

children.text: sa eva dharmo dharmī cety anunmatto na bhāṣate ||
children.translated_text: No one not mad says that the very same thing is both property and property-bearer.

children.text: kartā yady upamānaṃ syān nyagbhūto 'sau kriyāpade
children.translated_text: If the agent were the standard of comparison, it is subordinated in the verb,
busy accomplishing its own action and unable to look to anything else.

children.text: yo limpaty amunā tulyaṃ tama ity api śaṃsataḥ
children.translated_text: If one says, 'Darkness is like him who smears with this,'

children.text: aṅgānīti na saṃbaddhaṃ so 'pi mṛgyaḥ samo guṇaḥ ||
children.translated_text: then 'the limbs' is not connected, and even that similar quality must still be sought.

children.text: yathendur iva te vaktram iti kāntiḥ pratīyate
children.translated_text: Just as, in 'your face is like the moon,' radiance is understood,

children.text: na tathā limpater lepād anyad atra pratīyate ||
children.translated_text: so here, from the smearing of 'smears,' nothing else is understood.
Therefore this verb 'smears,' whose agent is darkness and whose meaning is contact,
and whose object is limbs, should be accepted as thus being poetically supposed of a person.

children.text: manye śaṅke dhruvaṃ prāyo nūnam ityevamādibhiḥ
children.translated_text: By words such as 'I think,' 'I suspect,' 'surely,' 'probably,' and 'certainly,'
<s>utprekṣā</s> is suggested; the word 'as if' also is of that kind.

children.text: hetuś ca sūkṣmaleśau ca vācām uttamabhūṣaṇam
children.translated_text: <s>Hetu</s>, along with the subtle and the slight, is an excellent ornament of speech;
causes are of two kinds, producing and indicating, and those are of many sorts, as follows:
This <s>Malaya</s> wind, shaking the shoots of mature sandal trees,
produces delight in everyone.
Here the strengthening of a form capable of producing delight
is specified as an ornament; even when there is cessation, it is the same.
Having shaken the sandal forest and touched the mountain streams of <s>Malaya</s>,
this wind has arrived for the non-existence of travelers.
For such a wind is indeed sufficient to bring about non-existence
in people who, afflicted by fever born of separation, have a charming aversion.

children.text: nivartye ca vikārye ca hetutvaṃ tadapekṣayā
children.translated_text: With respect to what is to be ended and what is to be changed, causality is relative to that;

children.text: prāpye tu karmaṇi prāyaḥ kriyāpekṣaiva hetutā ||
children.translated_text: but with respect to an object to be obtained, causality generally depends only on the action.
The cause of what is to be produced has been shown; of the remaining two,
Having given the pair of examples, the indicative cause will be described.
The forests have fresh shoots; the ponds have fully blossomed lotuses;

children.text: candraḥ pūrṇaś ca kāmena pānthadṛṣṭer viṣaṃ kṛtam ||
children.translated_text: and the moon is full: by Love they have been made poison for the traveler's sight.
Thinking, "I shall make her worthy of respect," the young woman looks at her friend, who stands in her beloved's place,
with her brows bent, her eyes crooked, and her lip quivering.

children.text: gato 'stam arko bhātīndur yānti vāsāya pakṣiṇaḥ
children.translated_text: The sun has set, the moon shines, and the birds go to their roosts:
this too is quite proper in indicating the condition of the time.
By the heats of your body, not to be killed by the moon's rays and not to be cured by sandal-water,

children.text: dehoṣmabhiḥ subodhaṃ te sakhi kāmāturaṃ manaḥ ||
children.translated_text: your love-tormented mind, friend, is easy to understand.
Thus, in poetic usages, charming indicative causes are to be recognized.
Certain delightful causes of absence are now stated.
Through lack of practice in the sciences, through lack of association with the wise,
and through lack of restraint of the senses, ruin arises for men.
The madness of talk about desire is gone; the fever of youth has passed away;

children.text: kṣato mohaś cyutā tṛṣṇā kṛtaṃ puṇyāśrame manaḥ ||
children.translated_text: delusion is wounded, thirst has fallen away, and my mind has been placed in a holy hermitage.

children.text: vanāny amūni na gṛhāṇy etā nadyo na yoṣitaḥ
children.translated_text: These are forests, not houses; these are rivers, not women;

children.text: mṛgā ime na dāyādās tan me nandati mānasam ||
children.translated_text: these are deer, not heirs: therefore my mind rejoices.
Conduct not examined beforehand is utterly improper for noble people;
therefore all their prosperities constantly increase.
Among the mango trees in the pleasure gardens not a single blossom-cluster has burst forth;
a libation of water with sesame should be offered for the women travelers.
Here the causal status of a thing whose form is prior absence and the like
is with respect to producing an effect whose nature is either presence or absence.
Remote effects, those born together with it, and those born immediately after an effect,
as well as effects that are unfitting and fitting: such varied causes are innumerable.
These, relying on secondary usage in the paths of poetic application,
are seen to be exceedingly beautiful; their examples are as follows.
That victorious weapon of <s>Anaṅga</s> called your sidelong glance, lady,

children.text: muktaṃ tad anyatas tena so 'py ahaṃ manasi kṣataḥ ||
children.translated_text: was released elsewhere by him; yet even I have been wounded in the heart by it.
The age of women, with childhood set aside, appears
together with the various bewilderments of love-madness in men.
Only afterward does the moon's disk, spreading out its rays, rise;
but before it, the ocean of passion in doe-eyed women has already risen.
How could the lotus-hands of kings be made into buds,
O lord, while touched by the tender dawn-redness of your pair of feet?
The rays of the moon-like nails of your feet, pure as jasmine,
are able to make the lotus-hands of kings close.
Thus such a procedure for the varieties of cause has been shown.
A meaning recognizable from gesture and appearance is called sūkṣma (subtle), because of its delicacy.

children.text: kadā nau saṃgamo bhāvīty ākīrṇe vaktum akṣamam
children.translated_text: Unable to say, in a crowded place, "When will our meeting be?",
the woman, understanding her beloved, closed her play-lotus.
Here, by the closing of the lotus, a meeting at night was indicated
by her who wished to reassure her beloved, afflicted by love.
While her gaze was fixed upon me in the musical gathering,
some hue on her lotus-face increased, trembling with intense passion.
Thus, because its form had not fully appeared, the desire for the festival of love
remained established here without overstepping subtlety.
Leśa is the concealment of the nature of a thing, though it is partly revealed by a part.
The form of this will become manifest in the example itself.
"The guards might understand that I am in love with the princess from my bristling hairs;

children.text: avagaccheyur ā jñātam aho śītānilaṃ vanam ||
children.translated_text: ah, this forest has a cold wind": so it should be understood.

children.text: ānandāśru pravṛttaṃ me kathaṃ dṛṣṭvaiva kanyakām
children.translated_text: "How have tears of joy begun to flow in me just from seeing the maiden?
My eye has been irritated by flower pollen stirred up by the wind."
In such cases and the like this ornament shines greatly.

children.text: leśam eke vidur nindāṃ stutiṃ vā leśataḥ kṛtām ||
children.translated_text: Some understand leśa as blame, or praise, made by a slight indication.

children.text: yuvaiṣa guṇavān rājā yogyas te patir ūrjitaḥ
children.translated_text: "This young king is virtuous, mighty, and a suitable husband for you;

children.text: raṇotsave manaḥ saktaṃ yasya kāmotsavād api ||

Here praise of the excellence of his valor is actually blame, meant to remove the feeling
of a girl who constantly wishes to enter into pleasures.

children.text: capalo nirdayaś cāsau janaḥ kiṃ tena me sakhi
children.translated_text: "That person is fickle and merciless; what use have I for him, friend,
when flatteries have been learned by him only for wiping away offenses?"
A seeming fault, namely skill in flattery, has been shown as a certain virtue
by a woman unable, because of passion, to maintain the pride urged on her by her friends.
The non-repetition, in order, of the objects that have been mentioned

children.text: yathāsaṃkhyam iti proktaṃ saṃkhyānaṃ krama ity api ||
children.translated_text: is called yathāsaṃkhya (correspondence in order); it is also called saṃkhyāna (enumeration) and krama (sequence).
Surely, slender one, your smile, your glance, and the radiance of your face
were stolen, when you entered the water to bathe, by the white lotus, the blue lotus, and the red lotus.
Preyas is the declaration of what is dear and dearer; rasavat is tender with rasa;

children.text: ūrjasvi rūḍhāhaṃkāraṃ yuktotkarṣaṃ ca tat trayam ||
children.translated_text: ūrjasvin is marked by established self-assertion; yuktotkarṣa is fitting excellence: these are the three.

children.text: adya yā mama govinda jātā tvayi gṛhāgate
children.translated_text: "<s>Govinda</s>, the affection that has arisen in me today, when you have come to my house,
will in time arise again only through your own coming."

children.text: ity āha yuktaṃ viduro nānyatas tādṛśī dhṛtiḥ
children.translated_text: So spoke <s>Vidura</s>, fittingly; from no other source could there be such firmness.
And <s>Hari</s>, who is propitiated by devotion alone, was therefore highly pleased.

children.text: somaḥ sūryo marudbhūmir vyoma hotānalo jalam
children.translated_text: "The moon, the sun, wind, earth, space, the sacrificer, fire, and water:

children.text: iti rūpāṇy atikramya tvāṃ draṣṭuṃ deva ke vayam ||
children.translated_text: O lord, who are we to behold you after passing beyond these forms?"

children.text: iti sākṣātkṛte deve rājño yad rātavarmaṇaḥ
children.translated_text: Thus, when the god was directly manifest, the expression of affection

children.text: prītiprakāśanaṃ tac ca preya ity avagamyatām ||
children.translated_text: by King <s>Ratavarman</s> should also be understood as preyas.

children.text: mṛte 'ti pretya saṃgantuṃ yayā me maraṇaṃ matam
children.translated_text: Thinking, "When she has died, I shall meet her after death," I considered death for myself.

children.text: saivāvantī mayā labdhā katham atraiva janmani ||
children.translated_text: That very <s>Avantī</s> has been obtained by me; how is this possible in this very life?

children.text: prāk prītir darśitā seyaṃ ratiḥ śṛṅgāratāṃ gatā
children.translated_text: The affection shown earlier has now become love, taking on the character of erotic sentiment,

children.text: nigṛhya keśeṣv ākṛṣṭā kṛṣṇā yenāgrato mama

children.text: so 'yaṃ duḥśāsanaḥ pāpo labdhaḥ kiṃ jīvati kṣaṇam ||
